sec.title: Background and purpose
sec.p: To evaluate the efficacy of surface-guided radiation therapy (SGRT) combined with real-time position management (RPM)-guided deep inspiratory breath-hold (DIBH) radiotherapy for left breast cancer.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: Twenty patients diagnosed with breast cancer, who underwent breast-conserving surgery and subsequent DIBH radiotherapy, were randomly assigned to two treatment groups: SGRT-guided (SGRT); and combined SGRT + RPM-guided (SGRT + RPM). Recorded setup and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) validation execution Time (T1), Beam delivery time (T2). Residual vertical setup error (VRT Error), six-dimensional (6D) setup errors, and breath-hold error (BH Error) were obtained using breath hold CBCT. Correlations between BH Error and VRT Error were analyzed. Dose reconstruction was performed using velocity-generated adaptive CT to compute per-fraction and accumulated doses, with coefficient of variation (CV) analysis used to quantify interfractional dose variations in clinical target volume (CTV) and organs at risk (OARs).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The mean (± SD) T1 and T2 times for the SGRT and SGRT + RPM groups were 452.53 ± 83.57 s vs. 299.58 ± 53.52 s (p < 0.05), and 147.85 ± 46.35 s vs. 135.3 ± 32.97 s (p > 0.05), respectively, with no statistical difference in 6D setup errors (p > 0.05). The SGRT group exhibited a mean BH Error that was 0.4 mm larger than that of the SGRT + RPM group, with a 0.7 mm reduction in stability. There was a correlation between BH Error and VRT Error in the SGRT group (r = 0.635, p < 0.05). Accumulated dose analysis revealed statistically significant decreases in CTV D98% and V95% in both groups (p < 0.05). However, maintained CTV coverage meeting clinical acceptability criteria (V95% ≥ 95%). The accumulated OARs doses demonstrated no significant differences compared with the planned doses (p > 0.05). There was no significant difference in CV values between the two groups (p > 0.05).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The DIBH guided by SGRT + RPM simplify the radiotherapy workflow, improve the operation efficiency and breath-hold (BH) quality of patients. Simultaneously, it guaranteed alignment of the cumulative doses received by the CTV and OARs with the planned doses.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy among women globally [1]. Although crucial for tumor control, postoperative radiotherapy poses a significant risk for radiation-induced organ damage [2]. This complication primarily stems from the unavoidable exposure of the cardiac and pulmonary structures to radiation fields, particularly in cases of left-sided breast cancer. Large-scale clinical studies have established a linear correlation between the mean heart dose and the incidence of radiation-induced cardiotoxicity [3]. Emerging evidence indicates that radiation exposure to critical cardiac substructures, especially the left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD), is an independent predictor of cardiovascular complications [4]. Consequently, optimizing treatment strategies to minimize radiation exposure to cardiac structures and their critical substructures has become the central focus of breast cancer radiotherapy research.

DIBH has emerged as an effective respiratory motion management technique for radiotherapy. This protocol requires patients to maintain deep inspiration during treatment delivery, inducing thoracic cage expansion and consequent cardiac displacement in the posterior-inferior direction. This geometric alteration not only enhances the spatial separation between target volumes (breast/chest wall) and critical cardiopulmonary structures but also reduces the proportional volume of irradiated lung tissue through volumetric expansion without altering the absolute irradiated volume. Multiple randomized trials have demonstrated that DIBH significantly mitigates radiation-induced cardiotoxicity and pulmonary complications, making it particularly beneficial for patients with early stage left breast cancer undergoing whole-breast irradiation after breast-conserving surgery [5–9].

Computer-assisted DIBH techniques encompass multiple advanced respiratory gating systems, including the following. The ABC system (Elekta, Stockholm, Sweden) actively controls the cessation of pulmonary ventilation and initiates radiotherapy when the patient’s inhalation volume reaches a predefined threshold [10]. The RPM system (Varian Medical Systems, Palo Alto, CA, USA), monitors respiratory motion via infrared tracking of a reflective module, using vertical amplitude to determine breath-hold consistency [11]. The SGRT system (AlignRT, Vision RT, London, United Kingdom) using a tri-camera infrared system to reconstruct three-dimensional surface topography enables six-degree-of-freedom motion tracking with submillimeter precision—a non-ionizing monitoring solution particularly advantageous for repeated exposure scenarios [12–14].

A recognized limitation of the ABC system is its reliance on spirometrically measured lung volumes as surrogate metrics for thoracic wall positioning. Clinical efficacy remains contingent on patient compliance and reproducibility of the breath-hold (BH) maneuver. Inconsistent respiratory gating may compromise the precision of target immobilization, potentially leading to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes [15]. The RPM system monitors only one-dimensional (1D) motion along the vertical direction, and during the transition from free breathing (FB) to DIBH, the heart and chest are displaced in three dimensions (3D; vertical, longitudinal, and lateral) [16]. Single-point 1D tracking may generate false BHs [17], and the RPM system cannot detect patient positioning offsets, leading to positioning errors in the vertical direction and causing significant dose deviations [18]. Therefore, accurate patient positioning and BH status can only be ensured through pre-treatment BH CBCT. However, the ionizing radiation emitted by CBCT limits its use. The SGRT system first uses the patient’s FB body surface to assess and correct six-dimensional (6D) setup errors, and then switches to the patient’s DIBH body surface to monitor the BH state and perform treatment. However, the SGRT workflow requires radiation therapists to repeatedly acquire and apply new DIBH reference surfaces, a process that can be complex when center couch-based BH CBCT verification is performed. Capturing a new reference surface after an image-guided patient setup, while simultaneously considering the correct BH level, can be challenging with DIBH SGRT [19–20]. Technical limitations of SGRT-guided BH therapy include the following: partial optical occlusion compromising surface tracking integrity; the patient’s BH level cannot be continuously monitored during couch movement; and possible residual errors in the vertical direction after FB setting. These systematic challenges have been identified as potential sources of respiratory-gating inaccuracies in SGRT [21].

As such, the present investigation developed SGRT combined with RPM-guided DIBH radiotherapy for left breast cancer, aiming to reduce setup and BH errors while improving treatment efficiency. Velocity 4.0 (Varian Medical Systems, USA) was used to perform an offline dose analysis of breast tumors and organs at risk (OARs) to confirm the feasibility of this protocol and provide a reference for clinical work.

sec.title: General patient information
sec.p: In accordance with the patient selection criteria for the DIBH technique in postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer proposed by Zhou et al. [22], 20 females diagnosed with left-sided breast cancer, who underwent breast-conserving surgery at the authors’ hospital between June 2024 and December 2024, were recruited for education and BH training. The inclusion criteria were as follows: The range of movement of the sternum in the anterior-posterior direction during BH(BH stability) < 3 mm; BH duration > 30 s; and the positional difference in the anterior-posterior direction of the sternum in DIBH and FB states > 8 mm. Patients were randomly assigned to one of two groups: SGRT guidance (SGRT); and SGRT combined with RPM guidance (SGRT + RPM). The SGRT group consisted of 10 patients (median age, 43.5 years [range, 29–63 years]), all with stage T1N0M0, and a median volume of breast gland target area of 486.05 cm³ (range, 257.1–768.89 cm³). The SGRT + RPM group included 8 patients (median age 46.5 years [range, 30–60 years]) with stage T1N0M0, 1 with stage T2N0M0, and 1 with stage T3N0M0, and a median volume of breast gland target area of 594.2 cm³ (range, 329.73–836.65 cm³). All patients had no other high-risk factors and only required whole-breast irradiation and tumor bed boost radiotherapy following breast-conserving surgery. None of the patients had contraindications to radiotherapy and all provided informed written consent before treatment.

sec.title: CT and plan design
sec.p: All patients were positioned supine, with their heads centered, arms raised, and abducted on a breast positioning system (Klarity Medical Co., Ltd., Guangzhou, Guangdong, China; model R610-DCF) with vacuum cushion fixation. Markers were placed on the skin in areas minimally affected by respiratory and arm movements. The RPM infrared reflection module was positioned at the center of the left thorax, and a marker was established on the skin. Under RPM guidance, CT was performed using a 16-slice Discovery RT CT simulator (GE Healthcare, Madison, WI, USA) in the FB and DIBH modes. The CT scan parameters were as follows: tube voltage, 120 kV; tube current, 440 mAs; and slice thickness, 2.5 mm. Two sets of CT images and BH curves were transferred to an Eclipse 15.6 3D planning system (Varian Medical Systems, USA). Target volumes and OARs were delineated on the DIBH CT datasets following standardized contouring guidelines for postoperative breast radiotherapy established by the National Cancer Center/Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences [23].

CTV was defined as the entire breast tissue identifiable on CT scan, assisted by wire markers placed around palpable breast tissue during the simulation. The CTV was limited posteriorly by the intercostal front and retracted 5 mm from the skin. The boost region (GTVtb) encompassed the surgical bed or seroma. The planning target volume (PTV) and PTVtb were expanded by 5 mm based on the CTV and GTVtb, excluding the heart. Both PTV and PTVtb were retracted 5 mm from the skin and limited posteriorly by the intercostal front to remove most of the build-up region for dose optimization and evaluation. The contoured OARs included the left lung (Lung-L), heart, LAD, right breast (Breast-R), spinal cord, and trachea. For all patients, a VitalBeam accelerator (Varian, USA) equipped with a millennium 120-leaf multileaf collimator, 6 MV flattening filter-free X-ray radiation, and a dose rate of 1400 monitor units/min was used. Using the Acuros XB algorithm with a 2.5-mm computational grid, the five to six tangential fields intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) technique was applied to minimize the irradiated volume of normal tissues. In accordance with the dose fractionation schema described by Wang et al. [24], the PTV received 42.56 Gy in 16 fractions (2.66 Gy/fx) delivered once daily for 3.2 weeks (5 fractions/week). This was followed by a sequential PTVtb boost of 8.7 Gy in three fractions (2.9 Gy/fx). Following the protocol described by Rossi [25], an 8-mm virtual bolus was integrated during plan optimization to mitigate target underdosing from respiratory motion, tissue edema, and anatomical deformation. This virtual bolus was excluded from final dose calculations.

sec.title: Pretreatment setup and plan execution
sec.p: For the SGRT group, a senior medical physicist transmitted the RT structures for both FB and DIBH CT simulations and RT plan files to the AlignRT system and outlined the surface of the sternum and portion of left breast as the infrared tracking region of interest (ROI) on both FB and DIBH body surfaces. For the SGRT + RPM group, only the RT structure was transmitted for FB CT simulations and RT plan files to the AlignRT system, and the surface of the sternum and portion of left breast outlined as the infrared tracking ROI on the FB body surface. Simultaneously, the infrared reflection module was positioned centrally on the left thorax for respiratory gating monitoring during breath holding. Based on a previous study [26], the gating tolerances were set at ± 0.3 cm in 1D for both the SGRT + RPM and SGRT groups, and at ± 0.3 cm translation and ± 3.0° rotation in 6D, respectively. The workflow for the two patient groups is illustrated in Fig. 1.

sec.title: Treatment efficiency, 6D setup error, vertical residual error, and BH error analysis
sec.p: Both patient groups underwent weekly acquisition of 360° complete BH CBCT verification imaging under the center couch. The total time from the initiation of patient setup to the commencement of treatment, including setup, CBCT image acquisition, registration analysis, couch movement, and body surface acquisition, was recorded as the Setup and CBCT Validation execution time (T1). The duration from the start to the completion of the beam delivery was recorded as the beam delivery time (T2). These metrics (T1 and T2) were used to evaluate the efficiency of the patient setup and image guidance as well as the treatment efficiency. In the treatment isocenter cross-sectional plane before BH CBCT registration, the deviation between CBCT and plan CT in the vertical direction at the anterior edge of the thoracic vertebrae was defined as the residual vertical setup error (VRT Error) (Fig. 2a). Before the treatment session, thoracic spine-based bone registration was performed, and the results were used to assess inter-fraction setup errors in 6D: vertical (Vrt), longitudinal (Lng), lateral (Lat), table rotation (Rtn), table tilt (Pitch), and table roll (Roll). After registration, in the patient’s treatment isocenter cross-sectional plane, the measurement of the distance between the spine and the sternum is defined as the breath-hold level, and the breath-hold level deviation between CBCT and planned CT was defined as the breath-hold error (BH Error).The mean of BH Error represents the average breath-hold error, while the standard deviation reflects breath-hold stability. The correlation between BH Error and VRT Error was analyzed in both patient groups.

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: Metrics data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to test data normality. For normally distributed data, paired t-tests were used for comparisons of related samples, independent sample t-tests were used for inter-group comparisons, and repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for comparisons of repeated measurement data. For non-normally distributed data, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for comparisons of related samples, and the Mann–Whitney U test was used for inter-group comparisons of independent samples. Correlations between 2 variables were assessed using the Spearman’s bivariate correlation process. Statistical calculations were performed using SPSS version 16.0 (SPSS Inc, Chicago, IL, USA). Differences with p < 0.05 were considered to be statistically significant.

sec.title: Treatment efficiency analysis (Fig. 4)
sec.p: The SGRT + RPM group exhibited significantly shorter total workflow duration for setup and CBCT validation (299.58 ± 53.52 s vs. 452.53 ± 83.53 s; p < 0.05), representing a 153-s time advantage over the protocol for the SGRT group. Beam delivery time demonstrated comparable efficiency between groups (SGRT, 147.85 ± 46.35 s vs. SGRT + RPM, 135.3 ± 32.97 s; p > 0.05), confirming equivalent treatment execution efficiency across both protocols.

sec.title: 6D setup error analysis
sec.p: Both groups underwent four BH CBCT scans per patient. 6D setup errors for the SGRT and SGRT + RPM groups were quantified as follows (translational: Vrt, 0.07 ± 0.25 cm vs. 0.04 ± 0.25 cm; Lng, -0.02 ± 0.31 cm vs. -0.07 ± 0.33 cm; Lat, -0.03 ± 0.27 cm vs. 0.03 ± 0.25 cm; rotational: Pitch, 0.06 ± 1.19° vs. -0.51 ± 1.03°; Roll, -0.14 ± 1.37° vs. 0.09 ± 1.14°; and Rtn, 0.25 ± 1.40° vs. -0.08 ± 1.21°). Inter-group comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences (p > 0.05).

Statistical histograms of the setup errors in the 6D direction for both groups are presented in Fig. 5. In the 3D translational directions, there was a situation where the error in the three-dimensional translation direction exceeded 0.5 cm; the maximum number of occurrences in the Lng direction for the SGRT and SGRT + RPM groups were five and four, respectively; in the SGRT group, the same patient had three occurrences in the Lat direction; in the SGRT + RPM group, the same patient had two occurrences in the VRT direction. The SGRT group had three cases exceeding 3° in the Roll direction, and both groups had one case each exceeding 3° in the Rtn direction.

sec.title: BH error analysis
sec.p: The SGRT group demonstrated a VRT Error of -0.09 ± 0.21 cm and BH Error of -0.04 ± 0.22 cm, compared with − 0.06 ± 0.22 cm (VRT Error) and 0.00 ± 0.15 cm (BH Error) for the SGRT + RPM protocol. There was no significant difference between the 2 groups (p > 0.05) (and a negative VRT Error indicated the need to raise the couch, while a positive value indicated the need to lower the couch; a negative BH Error indicated over-breath-hold, while a positive value indicated insufficient breath-hold). The average BH Error for Group SGRT was 0.4 mm more over-breath-hold compared with the SGRT + RPM group, with a decrease in BH stability of 0.7 mm. The SGRT group had six instances of over BH and one instance of insufficient BH exceeding the 3 mm threshold, whereas no such instances were found in the SGRT + RPM group. A scatter plot of the BH Error and VRT Error for both groups is presented in Fig. 6. In the SGRT group, the BH Error was positively correlated with the VRT Error (r = 0.635, p < 0.05). In the SGRT + RPM group, the BH Error was not correlated with the VRT Error (p > 0.05).

sec.title: Dosimetric analysis
sec.p: A comparison of the accumulated doses received by the CTV and OARs groups with the originally planned doses is presented in Table 1. For the SGRT and SGRT + RPM groups, the actual minimum dose received (D98%) for CTV decreased by an average of 20.1 cGy and 33.1 cGy, respectively (p < 0.05). In the SGRT + RPM Group, the average CTV volume with a dose of at least 95% prescription (V95%) decreased by 0.23% (p < 0.05). In the SGRT group, most OARs indices showed slight increases, except for LAD V40 and Lung-L V30. However, only V5 showed a statistically significant difference (p = 0.05). In the SGRT + RPM group, most OARs indices decreased, except for Lung-L V20, Breast Dmean, and LAD V40, which increased slightly. Notably, only the heart V10 exhibited a statistically significant difference (p < 0.05).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In DIBH radiotherapy for left breast cancer, SGRT demonstrates a strong correlation with CBCT in quantifying 6D setup errors [28–29], while outperforming both surface markers in error reduction/operational efficiency and three-point laser systems in positioning precision [30–31]. The SGRT + RPM workflow developed in this study specifically used the 6D positioning capability of the SGRT to address these technical requirements. SGRT shows a stronger correlation with actual target positions than RPM [32] and can detect intra‑fractional motion during breath‑hold that is not captured by volume‑based monitoring systems [33]. However, in breast cancer DIBH radiotherapy, surface data from SGRT include both positional offsets and breath‑hold errors, making it difficult to distinguish between the two. In this study, SGRT and RPM were used to monitor positional offsets and respiratory state, respectively. During treatment delivery, the SGRT system continued free-breathing surface tracking and recorded 6D positional data after breath‑hold release to evaluate potential offsets. Lu et al. [16] reported a non‑significant trend toward smaller cardiac positional deviations with SGRT guidance compared to RPM in tangential breast irradiation. Ono et al. [34] demonstrated stable DIBH maintenance using RPM by analyzing cine‑EPID images of the chest wall position relative to DRR references in the vertical field direction. Together, these findings support the feasibility of combining SGRT with RPM for breath‑hold radiotherapy in left‑sided breast cancer.Zhao et al. [35] showed that both thoracic and abdominal DIBH techniques significantly reduced doses to the heart, LAD artery, and left lung while maintaining target coverage. Their follow‑up study [36] further confirmed the superior organ‑at‑risk sparing of abdominal DIBH over thoracic DIBH. However, SGRT guidance relies on detectable chest wall motion generated by thoracic breathing, which inherently limits its use in patients who adopt an abdominal breathing pattern. SGRT combined with the RPM workflow can overcome this constraint through abdominal placement of the infrared reflector of the RPM for respiratory monitoring combined with SGRT-based thoracic surface surveillance, yielding wider clinical applicability. These technical considerations support the clinical adoption of SGRT combined with the RPM guidance protocol for DIBH radiotherapy in breast cancer.

Lorchel et al. [37] conducted a retrospective analysis of treatment workflow parameters for 22 patients with left-sided breast cancer treated using SGRT (AlignRT) on the Halcyon™ platform, reporting mean setup, CBCT verification, and total treatment session durations of 4, 1.1, and 14 min, respectively. The combined protocol (SGRT + RPM group) demonstrated a total workflow duration of 5 min for setup and CBCT verification, similar to literature reports. In contrast, the SGRT-only group exhibited a 50% increase in the total workflow duration (7.5 min). Compared with the SGRT + RPM group, the SGRT group required an additional step during positioning: moving the patient couch in 6 dimensions under DIBH conditions. Additionally, during BH CBCT verification, the SGRT group required two extra steps. First, the body surface for BH CBCT guidance was captured after the center couch and, second, after registration analysis, the patient couch was moved to the treatment isocenter under breath-hold conditions to capture the BH body surface. And the time the patient spends on repeatedly adjusting their breathing. These procedural differences resulted in a 2.5-min workflow prolongation for the SGRT group relative to the integrated SGRT + RPM protocol during positioning and CBCT verification.

Both groups demonstrated submillimeter/millidegree-level mean setup errors (≤ 1 mm/1°), with no statistical intergroup differences. Notably, critical deviations exceeding the 5-mm tolerance threshold were observed in both groups, predominantly along the longitudinal direction. These observation result may be due to the fact that when collecting the 6-dimensional couch movement data after the FB setup, the patient’s breathing fluctuations were significant. In the SGRT group, lateral deviations exceeding the 5-mm tolerance threshold occurred in a post-lumpectomy patient with a partial breast tissue deficit. To ensure the target dose coverage for the surgical cavity, pre-treatment a small piece of bolus was used in this region. This compensatory strategy inadvertently induces breast tissue deformation through bolus compression and generates lateral displacement. The SGRT + RPM group demonstrated vertical couch displacements exceeding the 5-mm tolerance threshold in one patient (two occurrences). This phenomenon may originate from treatment-induced thoracic cage elevation secondary to anxiety-related muscle tension during BH. Rotational errors have lower incidence rates and sporadic occurrences across cases, predominantly indicating stochastic error characteristics.

Numerous studies have demonstrated a residual error in the vertical direction when comparing initial SGRT with CBCT [38–40]. Two principal factors may contribute to the observed positional discrepancies: respiratory phase mismatch between real-time FB surface data and reference FB surfaces during the initial SGRT alignment when automatic couch translations are implemented; breast surface deformation-induced tracking uncertainties [41]. Although the SGRT group exhibited no significant differences in VRT and BH errors compared with the SGRT + RPM group, it experienced multiple instances of excessive or insufficient BH exceeding the 3-mm threshold. Additionally, the BH Error in the SGRT group was moderately correlated with the VRT Error. This may be attributed to the fact that the SGRT determines the vertical direction errors by measuring the absolute distance from the skin surface to the accelerator isocenter. When residual errors persist in the vertical direction after FB setup, they can influence the patient’s BH amplitude. In contrast, the SGRT + RPM group used RPM to measure the BH status and assess the amplitude of motion relative to the baseline. This relative measurement method was less susceptible to residual errors in the vertical direction. After performing the BH CBCT scan and registration, capture both DIBH and FB reference surface images can improve the VRT Error and BH Error. To reduce the influence of VRT Error on the BH value, multiple frames of the patient’s body surface during the entire respiratory cycle can be collected using SGRT. The mid-point of the patient’s respiratory cycle is used as the reference FB surface. This helps to minimize the VRT Error caused by the mismatch in respiratory phase between the real-time FB surface data and the reference FB surface. In addition to CBCT verification, Penninkhof et al. [39] and Tantan et al. [42] reported that visual feedback breathing training could improve BH errors. Dekker et al. [43] and Ucheng et al. [44] also suggested that BH stability improvements are associated with the width of the BH threshold; a narrower threshold range results in smaller breath-hold errors and enhanced BH stability.

Rossi et al. [45] reported − 2% to + 0.5% CTV coverage variations using CBCT-deformed CT datasets. While van der Veen et al. [46] observed modest PTV coverage reductions with CBCT-based anatomical modifications, Dekker et al. [43] achieved a CTV V95% coverage exceeding 98% in 90% of patients through CBCT-guided tangential/hybrid IMRT dose computation. Adaptive CT-based accumulated dose analysis revealed CTV D98% reductions of 1% (SGRT group) and 2% (SGRT + RPM group) compared with the planned doses. The SGRT + RPM group demonstrated a 0.7% decrease in the CTV V95%. Both groups maintained accumulated CTV V95% ≥ 95%, meeting clinical acceptability criteria for prescribed dose coverage. Beyond accumulated dose analysis, individual fraction dose distributions require critical evaluation. Hongo et al. [47] demonstrated a more pronounced target coverage degradation from vertical respiratory motion than from longitudinal displacements. Park et al. [48] quantified the directional setup error impacts in breast DIBH radiotherapy, revealing that longitudinal errors caused minimal heart/LAD dose alterations (< 5% variation) versus substantial cardiac dose elevation (49.4% of the planned dose) with 5 mm depth errors. Zellars et al. [49] identified greater interfraction variability in DIBH than in FB techniques, noting the cardiac immobilization risks of DIBH with prolonged high-dose exposure to specific myocardial regions, whereas FB induces dose blurring through respiratory motion. This dichotomy was further characterized by Wu et al. [50] using optical surface imaging. Large respiratory excursions in FB increased the risk(s) for target undercoverage, whereas DIBH elevated OARs doses to the lung, heart, and contralateral breast structures. Adaptive dose calculations per fraction demonstrated CTV V95% ≥ 95% for both groups, with CV ≤ 1% across all CTV dosimetric parameters. These findings confirm the capability of both groups to maintain stable CTV dose coverage (≥ 95% prescription) throughout the treatment course. Both groups exhibited Heart/LAD dose deviations from the planned values, demonstrating moderate interfraction variability (CV 15%–30%) without systematic directional bias. This pattern likely originates from normally distributed setup/BH errors (µ = -1 mm to + 1 mm) across fractions rather than unidirectional deviations. Furthermore, progressive dose blurring with increasing fractionation attenuated single-fraction positional/BH errors impacts on accumulated heart/LAD doses. The absence of significant discrepancies between the accumulated and planned heart/LAD doses in Table 1 corroborates this error self-compensation mechanism.

A limitation of this study is that it only included patients from our center, resulting in a relatively small sample size. Additionally, BH CBCT scans were captured weekly, which led to a slightly lower acquisition frequency. The cumulative dose was calculated as the mean of four physical doses without considering the potential for uneven irradiation between fractions, which could cause deviations in the biologically effective dose (BED). In the future, we plan to collaborate with multiple centers to increase the sample size and CBCT acquisition frequency. We incorporated the uneven irradiation of the CTV and OARs into our calculations and used the BED to compute the cumulative BED.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: SGRT + RPM-guided DIBH radiotherapy for left-sided breast cancer can simplify working steps, reduce BH errors, and improve work efficiency and BH stability. Although the dosimetric indices of the OARs exhibited varying degrees of fluctuation between fractionated treatments, the target volume received sufficient and stable dose coverage each time. Additionally, it ensured consistency between the cumulative doses received by the CTV and OARs and the original planned doses.
